questions.q: How does a tool call differ, as an action, from the actions trained in earlier chapters (tokens, full responses, reasoning steps)?
options: It is identical in every respect to a final text response
It never produces any output that affects future context
It ends the policy's turn and waits for an observation (the tool's result) to be returned and folded into context before the policy acts again, rather than waiting directly for a reward
It can only be used once per entire training run
questions.explain: A tool call's defining feature is that an external system's response becomes part of the state the policy conditions on for its next action, unlike a terminal action that simply ends the episode.

questions.q: What are the two components the lesson decomposes tool-use reward into?
options: Format/validity reward (is the tool call well-formed) and outcome reward (did the trajectory reach the correct final answer)
Token count and response latency
Model size and inference cost
Only a single outcome reward, with no other component
questions.explain: Tool-use reward splits into checking whether the call itself was syntactically/semantically valid and whether the overall trajectory's outcome was correct.

questions.q: In the lesson's tool_use_reward pseudocode, why does a well-formed but unsuccessful attempt get a small positive reward (0.1) instead of zero?
options: Because 0.1 is the maximum possible reward in this scheme
It is a bug that should be fixed
Because malformed calls also receive 0.1
To keep a good-faith, correctly formatted attempt that simply didn't succeed distinct from never attempting at all, which matters for later crediting of individual steps
questions.explain: A small non-zero reward preserves a useful distinction in the gradient signal between a reasonable attempt that failed and no attempt at all, which becomes important for multi-turn credit assignment in lesson 61.

questions.q: What does the ReAct pattern referenced in this lesson alternate between?
options: Randomly switching between two unrelated tasks
Producing reasoning text and producing an action (a tool call or final answer), with each tool call's result folded back into context before the next reasoning step
Training and evaluation phases within a single forward pass
Two separate policies trained independently
questions.explain: ReAct (Reason + Act) alternates reasoning steps with actions, using each returned observation to inform the next reasoning step.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what can RL training add on top of supervised imitation (SFT) of tool-use traces?
options: Nothing; SFT alone is always sufficient for tool use

The ability to discover task-success strategies absent from the imitation data, such as retrying with different arguments after an error or recognizing when no tool is needed, because RL's reward is tied to task success rather than resemblance to a reference trace
RL can only make the model imitate the training traces more exactly
RL removes the need for any tool schema validation
questions.explain: SFT optimizes for matching training traces; RL on top optimizes for actual task success, which can surface strategies that were never demonstrated in the imitation data at all.
